page.title: Knowledge Corner
page.description: SpotOptics is pleased to present information on the principles of their wavefront sensors and wavefront sensor based systems. You can learn more on Zernike polynomials, Shack Hartmann wavefront sensor comparison with interferometers, aberrations and photo gallery on aberrations. FAQ on SH test is also available.

articles.title: Shack-Hartmann vs. Hartmann Test
articles.caption: Hartmann Screen Test vs Shack-Hartmann Test Setup
articles.description: In the classical Hartmann test, a screen with holes is placed before the element being tested. The spots corresponding to these holes are recorded on a CCD, before or after the focus. The positions of these spots are mapped back onto the optical element, and the difference between the positions of these spots and the holes of the screen are used to compute the aberrations. This method is mostly obsolete now, as the Shack-Hartmann test has replaced it.

details.subtitle: A technical comparison of classical Hartmann screen testing and modern Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensors, highlighting calibration advantages, precision, and sensitivity.

hartmann_test.title: Hartmann Test
hartmann_test.description: In the classical Hartmann test, a screen with holes is placed before the element being tested. The spots corresponding to these holes are recorded on a CCD, before or after (as in the figure at right) the focus. The positions of these spots are mapped back onto the optical element, and the difference between the positions of these spots and the holes of the screen are used to compute the aberrations. This method is mostly obsolete now, as the Shack-Hartmann test has replaced it.

shack_hartmann_test.title: Shack-Hartmann Test
shack_hartmann_test.description: In the Shack-Hartmann test , a lenslet array is placed in the transferred pupil: light from the optical system being tested comes to a focus and is made parallel by the collimator, which also images the pupil on the array.
shack_hartmann_test.aberration_analysis: The displacements, shown by red arrows, due to the aberrations from the optical system, with respect to the ideal wavefront, shown by black arrow, are used to compute the aberrations (in terms of Zernike polynomials) and the wavefront.

technology_history.title: Application of Shack-Hartmann Technology
paragraphs: The Shack-Hartmann technology was first applied to the <a target='_blank' href='https://www.eso.org/sci/facilities/lasilla/telescopes/ntt.html'>ESO 3.5mt NTT Astronomical telescope<a/>.
Since ESO is a Scientific European Consortium the technology cannot be patented.
We acknowledge ESO scientists R. N. Wilson and L. Noethe for being the first who applied this technology to Astronomy.

comparison.title: Why Shack-Hartmann is Better
comparison.description: The Shack-Hartmann system is easier to calibrate and is of much higher precision compared to the Hartmann method. The use of a lenslet array leads to higher sensitivity.
advantages: Higher sensitivity through the use of a lenslet array

spotoptics_sensors.title: SpotOptics Shack-Hartmann Wavefront Sensors
spotoptics_sensors.description: SpotOptics Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensors can test optical systems on-axis as well as off-axis. Some models are also suitable for laser metrology.

wavelength_range.description: Our instruments can test at different wavelengths in the range 193nm to 10.6 microns.

spotoptics_sensors.accessories: We also offer a complete set of accessories to make easier your optical setup.

key_points.title: Hartmann Test
key_points.description: Uses a screen with holes and records corresponding spots on a CCD to calculate optical aberrations.

key_points.title: Shack-Hartmann Test
key_points.description: Uses a lenslet array and measures spot displacements relative to the ideal wavefront.

key_points.title: Higher Precision
key_points.description: The Shack-Hartmann system provides much higher precision compared to the classical Hartmann method.

key_points.title: Higher Sensitivity
key_points.description: The lenslet array provides higher sensitivity for wavefront measurements.

key_points.title: Wide Wavelength Range
key_points.description: SpotOptics instruments can test wavelengths ranging from 193nm to 10.6 microns.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.description: The Shack-Hartmann system has replaced the classical Hartmann test for many applications because it is easier to calibrate, provides higher precision and offers higher sensitivity through the use of a lenslet array.
conclusion.final_text: SpotOptics Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensors provide solutions for on-axis and off-axis optical testing, with selected models also suitable for laser metrology.

zygo_comparison.title: SpotOptics Optino vs. Zygo Interferometer
zygo_comparison.description: A direct comparison between Zygo GPIxp HR interferometer measurements and SpotOptics Optino/SenSoft wavefront sensor results.
bullets: A small area (7 mm) of a hard-disk platter was tested using the Zygo GPIxp HR (high resolution) interferometer.
The same area was tested with our standard instrument Optino/SenSoft.
A high-quality lambda/20 flat mirror was used for the calibration.
Both tests were done in double pass at 632.8 nm.

overview.title: Why Long Focal Length Matters
paragraphs: We explain the importance of using Shack-Hartmann lenslet arrays with long focal length using a simulation computed with our Sensoft simulation package.
10 nm of Coma are added to a perfect wave (Standard Zernike coefficients).
The spot displacements on the normalized pupil are computed for two different cases.

items.title: Standard lenslet array
items.description: Assuming our standard lenslet array with focal length = 22 mm.

items.title: Generic array
items.description: Assuming a generic array with focal length = 5 mm.

simulation_result.description: The result shows that the length of the displacement is proportional to the focal length. It is therefore easier to detect Coma when fl = 22 mm.

noise_simulation.title: Effect of Random Noise
paragraphs: An additional simulation is performed by adding 0.2 micron random noise to the spot displacements for the two cases.
In the presence of modest noise, with fl=5 mm the Coma displacements disappear inside the noise, while for fl=22 mm the Coma pattern is still visible in the displacements.

figure_1.title: Spot displacements due to Coma aberration
figure_1.description: Spot displacements due to Coma aberration (PV = 48 nm) that one can expect using Shack-Hartmann lenslet array with focal length fl = 22 mm (our standard choice, left) and fl = 5 mm (right).

figure_2.title: Adding Random Noise
figure_2.description: Adding random noise of max 0.2 um. For lenslet array with focal length fl = 5 mm (right) the displacements are inside the noise while for fl = 22 mm (left) the Coma pattern is still visible in the displacements.

items.description: Gives unstable and unreliable results since it is very poor in resolving aberrations especially in presence of noise and also causes thermal instability as the lenslet array is too close to the camera chip and often INSIDE the camera body.

articles.title: Zernike Polynomials in Sensoft
articles.caption: Zernike polynomials used in Sensoft - our wavefront sensor software
articles.description: Zernike polynomials represent a particular phase aberration W at a point P on a circular pupil and they are generally expressed in terms of the normalized radius r of the pupil and the azimuthal angle φ, by the following expression: rⁿ cos(mφ + φ₀).

details.page_discription: Accurately represent and analyze phase aberrations with Sensoft's advanced wavefront modeling. Whether you need standard mathematical fitting or need to account for central optical obscurations, our software adapts to your exact measurement needs.

paragraphs: This is the general expression in terms of the Seidel  polynomials. The Standard Zernike polynomials, on the other hand, involve aberration balancing, in which aberrations of a lower order are combined with those of the higher order for reducing the wavefront error. For example, the expression for 3rd order spherical aberration also contains a defocus term.  φ0   is the zero-offset : it gives the orientation of the particular aberration with respect to the x-axis.

annular_zernike.title: Annular Zernike Polynomials
annular_zernike.description: Finally, the Annular Zernike polynomials also take into account the effect of the annulus ε of the optical element.

sensoft_selection.title: Zernike polynomial options in Sensoft
sensoft_selection.description: SpotOptics wavefront sensor software SenSoft allow you to select among four polynomials to fit to the data.

polynomial_types.title: Annular Zernike polynomials
polynomial_types.description: Annular Zernike polynomials are based on diffraction theory and take into account the presence of the central obscuration in the pupil. They are the most general form of Zernike polynomials. They are normally used in astronomical wavefront sensors (like Puntino) to take into account the obscuration by the secondary mirror of the telescope.

polynomial_types.title: Standard Zernike polynomials
polynomial_types.description: Standard Zernike polynomials follow from Annular Zernike polynomials, with the central obscuration factor, and are normalized over the pupil.

polynomial_types.title: Fringe Zernike polynomials
polynomial_types.description: Fringe Zernike polynomials are the same as Standard Zernike polynomials without the normalization factors. They are mainly used in the field of interferometry, as suggested by the name.

polynomial_types.title: Seidel polynomials
polynomial_types.description: The Seidel polynomials are the extension of Seidel aberrations from geometrical optics.

summary.title: Summary
summary.description: Zernike polynomials provide a mathematical representation of wavefront aberrations over a circular pupil. Sensoft provides multiple polynomial conventions for fitting wavefront sensor data, including Annular Zernike, Standard Zernike, Fringe Zernike and Seidel polynomials.
